Informal means relaxed, casual, and free from strict rules, official structure, or ceremony. It describes situations, language, clothes, relationships, or arrangements that are not bound by rigid formality — things that feel natural, loose, and easy rather than stiff, official, or ceremonious.

To truly understand "informal," you first need to understand what formal means, because "informal" is built as its direct opposite.
Formal vs. Informal — The Contrast That Unlocks Everything

Think of formal as a world with clear, strict rules about how things must be done — with ceremony, official structure, and a sense of seriousness. Now, informal is the world without those strict rules. It is the relaxed, everyday, people-being-people version of things.

Imagine two dinners:

Dinner A: You sit at a grand table with a white tablecloth. Everyone wears suits and gowns. You address people as "Sir" or "Madam." There is a fixed order of events — welcome speech, three courses, a toast. Nobody kicks off their shoes. → This is formal.

Dinner B: You sit on a couch with friends. Everyone wears jeans. You call each other by first names or nicknames. You eat pizza from the box. Someone laughs loudly and nobody minds. → This is informal.

The same contrast runs through almost every area of life where "informal" is used.

It helps to think of a sliding scale:

Very Formal ←——————————————→ Very Informal

A military ceremony sits at the far left. A chat between best friends in a garden sits at the far right. Most things in life sit somewhere in between, leaning one way or the other. When something leans toward the casual, relaxed, unofficial side, we call it informal.
The Main Areas Where "Informal" Is Used

1. Language and Writing

This is one of the most common uses. Informal language is the way people speak in everyday conversation — with friends, family, or in casual settings. It uses:

  • Contractions: "I'm, don't, can't" (instead of "I am, do not, cannot")
  • Slang and everyday words: "kids" instead of "children," "guy" instead of "gentleman"
  • Loose grammar that reflects natural speech
  • Abbreviations in texting: "lol, btw, gonna"

A text message to a friend is informal. A cover letter for a job application is formal.

Informal writing doesn't follow all the strict rules of grammar and tone that formal writing demands. It feels like talking on paper. Neither is "wrong" — they simply serve different purposes and different audiences.

2. Clothes and Dress

Informal clothing (also called "casual wear") means clothes you wear in relaxed, everyday situations — jeans, t-shirts, sneakers, sundresses, hoodies. When an invitation says "informal dress," it means you should not wear a tuxedo or a ball gown. Come comfortable. Come as yourself.

Formal wear, by contrast, means suits, ties, gowns — clothes that signal seriousness and occasion.

3. Situations and Events

Some occasions are informal by nature — birthday parties, picnics, casual get-togethers, a relaxed team lunch. They have no strict program, no rigid protocol. People mingle freely, speak openly, and the mood is light.

Others — like a court hearing, a graduation ceremony, or a state banquet — are formal. They follow a fixed, serious structure.

4. Relationships

An informal relationship is one without official hierarchy or rigid roles dominating how people interact. You can speak freely, joke, and be yourself. A friendship is inherently informal. Even a professional relationship can be informal in tone — for example, a boss who encourages everyone to use first names, crack jokes, and speak openly in meetings.

A formal relationship, by contrast, is defined by titles, roles, and proper conduct — a judge and a lawyer in a courtroom, for instance.

5. Agreements and Arrangements

An informal agreement is one that is not written down, not legally binding, and not processed through any official system. It relies on mutual trust and a handshake rather than a signed contract. For example: "We had an informal understanding that he would help me move, and I'd cook dinner for him."

A formal agreement involves paperwork, legal language, signatures, and official record-keeping.

6. The Informal Economy (or Informal Sector)

In economics, the informal sector refers to work and business activity that happens outside official government regulation — no taxes filed, no official records, no contracts. Street vendors, casual day labor paid in cash, small unregistered businesses — these are part of the informal economy. It is a real and important concept used widely in social studies and economics.

7. Informal Learning and Education

Informal education or informal learning is the learning that happens outside a classroom or official institution — through experience, conversation, reading for pleasure, watching a documentary, or being mentored by someone. It has no syllabus, no grades, no certificate.

Formal education follows a structured system — schools, universities, curricula, examinations.

When something is informal, it tends to feel:

  • Relaxed — No pressure to perform or follow strict rules
  • Accessible — Easy to approach; not intimidating
  • Personal — Human, warm, and direct
  • Flexible — Adaptable, not rigid
  • Unofficial — Not processed through an authority or institution

These qualities are not negative. Informal is not lesser than formal. It is simply appropriate for different contexts.
An Important Nuance — Context Is Everything

"Informal" is not a judgment of quality. Informal does not mean bad, wrong, sloppy, or unprofessional. It simply means not formal. The key is choosing the right register for the right moment.

Speaking informally to a close friend is perfectly correct. Speaking informally in a formal job interview would be a mismatch — not because informal is bad, but because the context calls for something different.

Similarly, an informal settlement in urban planning refers to a neighbourhood that grew without official planning permission — like a shanty town or slum. No judgment about the people living there is implied. It simply describes the unofficial nature of how it came to exist.

The word is always about the nature of the thing (unstructured, unofficial, relaxed), not a judgment of its worth.

Here are expressions where "informal" naturally appears, so you recognise it in real use:

  • Informal meeting — A casual, unscheduled gathering, no formal agenda
  • Informal chat / talk — A relaxed conversation, not a structured discussion
  • Informal setting — A relaxed environment (a café, a living room) as opposed to a boardroom or court
  • Informal tone — A warm, conversational style of writing or speaking
  • Informal sector / economy — Work outside official government systems
  • Informal vote — In some countries, a ballot that doesn't follow the correct rules and so isn't counted
  • Keep it informal — A request to relax, not stand on ceremony
  • On an informal basis — Without official structure or commitment

Words that mean something similar to informal:
Casual, relaxed, unofficial, laid-back, colloquial (for language), everyday, unpretentious, off-the-record, impromptu, friendly

Words that mean the opposite:
Formal, official, ceremonial, structured, rigid, conventional, proper, professional
One-Line Summary to Anchor It All
Informal means relaxed, casual, and free from official rules or strict ceremony — the natural, everyday, unstructured side of things, as opposed to the formal, official, and rule-bound side.
